entry: Lake in East-central Africa, one of the [[African Great Lakes]], shared by [[Tanzania]], [[Uganda]] and [[Kenya]]. At 59,947 sq km, it is Africa's largest lake by area and the world's largest tropical lake. It is also the world's second-largest freshwater lake by surface area, after [[Lake Superior]] in North America. The lake has an average depth of 40 m and a maximum depth of 80–81 m. It is drained solely by the [[Nile|Nile River]] near Jinja, Uganda. In 1858, John Hanning Speke, the first Briton to document the lake, renamed it after [[Queen Victoria]] while on an expedition with Richard Francis Burton. Many [[Cichlid|cichlid]] fish species live nowhere else in the lake, but introduced Nile perch have driven many endemic species to extinction.

Artificial [[Reservoir|reservoir]] in [[Ghana]], the world's largest by surface area, covering 8,502 sq km. It lies entirely within Ghana and is held back by the Akosombo Dam, built between 1961 and 1965. The dam generates a substantial share of Ghana's electricity, producing 912 MW for domestic use and for export to [[Togo]], [[Benin]] and other nearby countries. Its formation flooded 15,000 homes in 740 villages, requiring the resettlement of 78,000 people. Resettlement was poorly organized, and the hardship it caused continued long after the project's completion. The lake disrupted traditional fishing and farming and caused a large spike in disease prevalence. It also opened a navigable route to the north and supports [[Tourism|tourism]]. Water levels have fallen recently, which is attributed to global warming, reducing power generation.

Subglacial lake in central East [[Antarctica]], the largest of the continent's 675 known subglacial lakes. It lies beneath Russia's Vostok Station, under about 4,000 m of ice and roughly 500 m below sea level. Russian geographer Andrey Kapitsa first suggested its existence from seismic soundings made in 1959 and 1964; J. P. Ridley confirmed it in 1993 using ERS-1 laser altimetry. The overlying ice holds a paleoclimatic record of 400,000 years, while the lake water may have been isolated for 15 to 25 million years. In 2012 Russian scientists pierced the ice, and water from the lake gushed up the borehole, mixing with Freon and [[Kerosene|kerosene]]. Some environmental groups and scientists argue that hot-water drilling would have a more limited environmental impact. The lake's isolated conditions may resemble those of ice-covered oceans on [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] and [[Enceladus]].

Large, shallow glacial lake in [[Manitoba]], Canada, whose southern end lies about 55 km north of [[Winnipeg|the city of Winnipeg]]. At 24,514 sq km, it is the 12th-largest lake on Earth, Canada's sixth-largest freshwater lake and the third-largest freshwater lake entirely within Canada. Its mean depth is 12 m, and its deepest section is a 36-m channel between the northern and southern basins. The watershed, about 982,900 sq km, receives water from four Canadian provinces and four U.S. states. The lake drains northward through the Nelson River, part of the [[Hudson Bay]] watershed. It is a remnant of Glacial Lake Agassiz. Its eastern side has boreal forests and rivers inscribed in 2018 as Pimachiowin Aki, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The lake supports 60 of the 79 native fish species found in Manitoba, more than any other lake in Canada west of the [[Great Lakes]].

Union territory of India, an archipelago of 36 islands in the [[Arabian Sea]]. The name means one hundred thousand islands in Malayalam and Sanskrit. Human settlement dates to at least 1500 BCE, and [[Islam]] is presumed to have reached the islands in the 7th century. In the 11th century the Chola kingdom influenced the islands, which lay on a trade route between the Middle East and South Asia. The British Empire annexed them in 1799; they became part of India in 1947 and a union territory in 1956. Fishing and agriculture are the main occupations, and [[Coconut|coconut]] cultivation and tourism are important.

Hindu god, younger half-brother of [[Rama]] in the epic [[Ramayana]]. Considered an incarnation of Shesha, the lord of serpents, he is known for his loyalty to Rama. He accompanied Rama during a 14-year exile, serving him and [[Sita]], and played a pivotal role in the war, killing Meghanada. He was married to Urmila. Lakshmana is worshipped in Hinduism at various places in India, alongside Rama and Sita. The name is [[Sanskrit]] for the one endowed with auspicious signs.

Major Hindu goddess of fortune, wealth, prosperity, beauty and fertility. Also known as Shri, she forms with Parvati and Sarasvati the goddesses called the Tridevi. In the late epic period, around 400 CE, she became associated with the preserver god [[Vishnu]] as his consort. Whenever Vishnu descended to earth as an avatar, she accompanied him, as [[Sita]] with [[Rama]] and Rukmini with [[Krishna]]. She is prominent in [[Vaishnavism]], where she is also Vishnu's divine energy, and in [[Shaktism]] she is venerated as the prosperity aspect of the supreme goddess. She is often shown with four arms, flanked by elephants and holding a lotus. The eight manifestations known as Ashtalakshmi symbolize eight sources of wealth. Festivals such as [[Diwali|Deepavali]] honor her.

Queen consort of the princely state of Jhansi and a leader of the [[Indian Rebellion of 1857]]. Born Manikarnika Tambe in [[Varanasi]], she was married at a young age to the raja of Jhansi, Gangadhar Rao, and took the name Rani Lakshmibai. After Gangadhar Rao died in 1853, the [[East India Company|British East India Company]] refused to recognize his adopted heir and annexed Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse. In May 1857 Indian troops at Jhansi mutinied and massacred most of the British in the town; the Rani's complicity is still disputed. She took over the rulership and fought several battles against the British until Major General Hugh Rose captured Jhansi in March and April 1858. She escaped on horseback and joined rebel leaders at Kalpi, then died in battle at Gwalior Fort. She is celebrated in modern India as a symbol of Indian nationalism, although [[Dalit]] communities tend to view her negatively.

Meat of the domestic [[Sheep|sheep]] (*Ovis aries*). Lamb comes from sheep in their first year, hogget from sheep in their second, and mutton from older sheep. Lamb is the most expensive of the three, and the stronger-tasting mutton is now hard to find in many areas. In Britain, lamb is defined by having no permanent incisor teeth. From July 1, 2019, [[Australia]] has defined lamb as animals under 12 months old or with no permanent incisors in wear. In central Italy, including the [[Lazio]] region, abbacchio, lamb still suckling or recently weaned, is a traditional [[Easter]] and Christmas dish, protected by the [[European Union|European Union]] with a PGI mark. In most of South and Southeast Asia, the term mutton is applied to goat meat.

Formal system of [[Mathematical logic|mathematical logic]] for expressing computation through function abstraction and application. Introduced by Alonzo Church in the 1930s, the untyped lambda calculus is a universal model of computation that can simulate any [[Turing machine]]. Its terms are variables, abstractions and applications, manipulated by transformation rules such as beta-reduction. Church found a logically consistent formulation in 1936 and documented it in 1940. The system is central to the semantics of [[Programming language|programming languages]] and to the theory of [[Functional programming|functional programming]].

Multivalued function, the converse relation of f(w) = w eʷ, also called the product logarithm. Johann Lambert considered a related problem in 1758, and [[Leonhard Euler]] described the function in 1783. For each integer k there is one branch, Wₖ(z), with W₀ the principal branch. For real numbers, only W₀ and W₋₁ are needed. Its branches cannot be expressed in elementary functions. The function is used in [[Combinatorics|combinatorics]], notably the enumeration of trees, and in solving equations with [[Exponential function|exponentials]], such as the maxima of the Planck, Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac distributions.

Family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] known as mints, deadnettles and sages. Most of its roughly 236 genera and 6,900 to 7,200 species are aromatic, and most are herbaceous. The family includes culinary herbs such as [[Basil|basil]], [[Mentha|mint]], [[Rosemary|rosemary]], sage and [[Thyme|thyme]], along with medicinal plants such as catnip and skullcap. Many are cultivated for their aromatic leaves, and some for seed, such as chia (*Salvia hispanica*), or for edible tubers. The largest genus, [[Salvia]], has 900 species. Flowers are bilaterally symmetrical, with petals fused into upper and lower lips, which gives the alternative name Labiatae.

Jawless fish of the order Petromyzontiformes, with about 38 extant species. Adults have a toothed, funnel-like sucking mouth, an elongated scaleless body and no paired fins. Most of a lamprey's life is spent as a juvenile ammocoete, burrowing into sediment and filter-feeding. Only 18 species are carnivorous, boring into other fish to feed on flesh and blood. Genetic evidence links lampreys to [[Hagfish|hagfish]], the other living group of jawless fish. The sea lamprey, an introduced pest in the [[Great Lakes]], has harmed native fish stocks, and control programs use lampricides and barriers.

Lao kingdom in [[Southeast Asia]] from 1353 to 1707. Founded by Fa Ngum in 1353, it was one of the largest kingdoms in the region for three and a half centuries. Its name, meaning the Million Elephants and the White Parasol, alluded to the power of its king, his ties to Buddhism and his army's war elephants. Its capital was Luang Prabang until 1560 and [[Vientiane]] thereafter. [[Theravada|Theravada]] Buddhism was the state religion, and the [[Mekong]] River carried its trade. Burma invaded in the sixteenth century, and in 1707 the kingdom was partitioned into Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak. It remains the basis of [[Laos]]'s national historic and cultural identity.

American singer-songwriter. She grew up in upstate New York and moved to [[Manhattan]] in 2005 to pursue a music career. Her major-label debut, *Born to Die* (2012), has a cinematic, hip-hop-inflected sound and became the longest charting album by a woman in the history of the US Billboard 200. Her later albums added psychedelic, orchestral and folk elements, and *Norman Fucking Rockwell!* (2019) was named one of the 500 greatest albums by [[Rolling Stone]]. She has received 11 Grammy Award nominations.

Ceremonial county in North West England (est. pop., 2024: 1,601,645). Its largest settlement is Preston, and its western edge meets the [[Irish Sea]]. The county covers 3,079 sq km, with coastal plains in the west and uplands in the east, including the Forest of Bowland. Founded in the 12th century, it became a palatine in 1351. During the [[Industrial Revolution]] it industrialized rapidly, with a large textile industry, and until 1974 it included [[Liverpool]] and [[Manchester]].

American former professional road racing cyclist, born in [[Texas]]. He won the [[Tour de France]] a record seven consecutive times, from 1999 to 2005. In 2012, a U.S. Anti-Doping Agency investigation concluded that he had used performance-enhancing drugs, and his titles were stripped. Armstrong denied the allegations but did not contest the charges, and he received a lifetime ban from sanctioned cycling. He founded the Lance Armstrong Foundation, now Livestrong, after recovering from metastatic testicular cancer. In 2018 he settled a civil lawsuit with the [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Department of Justice]], agreeing to pay US$5 million.

Explosive weapon, usually concealed under or on the ground, that detonates when a target passes over or near it. Anti-[[Tank|tank]] mines disable vehicles, while anti-personnel mines injure or kill people. Land mines are typically pressure-activated and laid throughout an area to form a minefield. Mines using [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]] as the explosive were used from the [[Ming dynasty]] to the [[American Civil War]], and high explosives were developed later. Their indiscriminate nature and their potential to remain dangerous long after a conflict has ended make their use controversial. The 1997 Ottawa Treaty, which bans anti-personnel mines, has been signed by 164 nations, but China, Russia and the United States are not signatories.

Ancient trading kingdom in the [[Horn of Africa]], known from Egyptian trade records. It produced and exported gold, aromatic resins, blackwood, ebony, ivory and wild animals. Recent evidence places it in northwestern [[Eritrea]], while most historians situate it in East Africa, in territories covering [[Somalia]], Sudan, Ethiopia and Eritrea. The earliest recorded Egyptian expedition was organized by [[Pharaoh]] Sahure of the Fifth Dynasty, in the 25th century BC. In the 15th century BC, [[Hatshepsut|Queen Hatshepsut]] sent a five-ship voyage whose outcome is shown in reliefs at her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri. Puntland, an autonomous region of Somalia, is named in its honor.

Process of creating new land from oceans, seas, riverbeds or lake beds. Early examples include a scheme by rulers of the Twelfth Dynasty (c. 2000–1800 BC), who built levees and canals to create farmland around the Faiyum in ancient Egypt. The [[Polder|Beemster Polder]] in the [[Netherlands]] added 70 sq km of land in 1612. Methods include infilling with heavy rock or cement, draining submerged wetlands for agriculture, and dredging sediments. Some 20% of land in the Tokyo Bay area has been reclaimed. The city of [[Rio de Janeiro]] was largely built on reclaimed land, as was [[Wellington]]. Reclaimed land is also called land fill, which is not the same as waste in a [[Landfill|landfill]].

Movement of people, animals and goods between places by land-based routes. It contrasts with [[Maritime transport|maritime transport]] and aviation, and its two main forms are [[Rail transport|rail]] and [[Road transport|road]] transport. Human-powered transport, including walking, running and cycling on [[Bicycle|bicycles]], remains popular for its low cost, leisure and environmental benefits. Animals serve as pack animals or pull sleds and wheeled vehicles. A train is hauled by a [[Locomotive]] that pulls unpowered cars, using steam, diesel or electricity. Road transport offers door-to-door service and flexibility, and [[Truck|trucks]] often handle the first and final stages of freight transport.

Site for the disposal of waste materials, including municipal solid waste. Burying waste is the oldest and most common form of disposal, though systematic burial with daily and final covers began only in the 1940s. Sanitary sites, introduced early in the 20th century, gained wide use in the 1960s and 1970s to replace open dumps. Operators confine and compact waste, then cover it daily with soil or other materials. Gases from the site contribute to climate change, and liquid leachates can contain high concentrations of polluting materials. Unless stabilized, a site may undergo severe shaking or soil liquefaction during an [[Earthquake|earthquake]]. Once full, the area may be reclaimed for other uses, and [[Recycling|recycling]] and [[Waste management|waste management]] can reduce the material sent to it.

Land feature on the solid surface of Earth or another planetary body. Landforms include hills, [[Mountain|mountains]], canyons and valleys, as well as shoreline features such as bays and peninsulas and submerged features such as [[Mid-ocean ridge|mid-ocean ridges]]. Hills, mountains, plains and [[Plateau|plateaus]] are the four major types on Earth. Tectonic movements can create landforms by pushing up hills and mountains, while [[Erosion|erosion]] and deposition, including human activity, also shape them. Biological factors matter too: vegetation shapes dunes and salt marshes, and corals and algae build reefs. The arrangement of landforms in a landscape is called topography, and their scientific study is [[Geomorphology|geomorphology]].

Design of outdoor areas, landmarks and structures to achieve environmental, social or aesthetic outcomes. The field spans public parks and parkways, campus and corporate site planning, stormwater management, erosion control and environmental restoration. It is multidisciplinary, drawing on [[Ecology|ecology]], [[Civil engineering|civil engineering]], horticulture, botany and urban design. Gilbert Laing Meason coined the term in 1828, and John Claudius Loudon helped establish it. Before 1800 the work was largely master planning for estates, such as André Le Nôtre's Gardens of Versailles for [[Louis XIV]] of France. [[Frederick Law Olmsted]] pioneered the profession in the United States, designing New York City's [[Central Park]] in 1858.

Depiction of natural scenery, such as mountains, valleys, rivers and forests, in painting. The elements usually form a coherent composition, and sky and weather are almost always included. Landscapes may be imaginary or copied from reality, and a view of a specific place with prominent buildings is called a topographical view. The earliest pure landscapes are Minoan frescos from around 1500 BCE. Roman landscape frescos and mosaics survive from the 1st century BCE onward, notably at [[Pompeii]] and Herculaneum. Two main traditions, Western and [[Chinese art|Chinese]], go back well over a thousand years; Chinese shan shui ink painting shows human life only as a sage or a glimpse of his hut. The spiritual element of landscape art became explicit in the West only with [[Romanticism]].
